items.abstract: <jats:p>The Stone Age marked the extensive use of rocks for tool-making, with flint as the primary material. However, prehistoric communities, ranging from the Early Lower Paleolithic to the Holocene, also utilized other stones like quartz due to their availability and suitability for manufacturing tools. Quartzose raw materials (quartz and quartzite) were widely exploited during prehistory, particularly in contexts where flint or other sources were scarce or unavailable. However, there are recorded findings of quartz tools from sites located in areas where flint sources were effectively accessible and exploited, such as at the Early Middle Paleolithic (EMP) site of Coudoulous I. This site presents a good opportunity to discuss the subsistence strategies and raw material procurement of Neanderthals in southwestern France and to explore methodological considerations related to the analysis of quartz assemblages. We examined 79 quartz and quartzite artifacts from layer 4 of a bone bed dating back to Marine Isotope Stage 6 (MIS 6), employing optical and digital microscopy along with a comprehensive reference collection. As a result, it was the most commonly identified activity. The hunting-oriented nature of the site is further supported by the limited evidence of other activities, apart from a few instances of scraping or cutting wood and dry hide, which are likely associated with the creation and maintenance of the tools used for hunting. Additionally, some quartz and quartzite artifacts with convergent edges display wear patterns consistent with their use as spear points. Therefore, the lithic industry at Coudoulous I highlights the significance of quartz and quartzite in EMP subsistence strategies and indicates that quartzose materials should not be undervalued or dismissed as opportunistic behavior.</jats:p>
items.summary: 《揭示石英与石英岩在法国库杜卢斯I遗址早中期旧石器时代野牛猎杀与屠宰场中的作用》：研究通过显微分析库杜卢斯I遗址第4层出土的79件石英和石英岩制品，探讨尼安德特人的生存策略与原料获取，发现狩猎是最主要的活动，部分制品用作矛头，表明石英质原料不应被低估或视为机会主义行为。
items.title: Unveiling the Role of Quartz and Quartzite at the Early Middle Paleolithic Bison Kill and Butchery Site of Coudoulous I (Quercy, France)

items.abstract: Glyptodonts (Xenarthra, Cingulata) were large and armoured herbivores forming part of the Cenozoic megafauna of the Americas. Numerous species were recognised based on differences in the ornamentation of their dorsal carapace osteoderms. Phylogenetic and morphological studies indicate that this high diversity was overestimated since many of the variations once used to define species actually reflect ontogenetic changes or taphonomic alterations. Here, we present a detailed revision of the enigmatic Neuryurus rudis (Gervais, 1878), considered a keyelement of the Ensenadan Age/Stage (Early Middle Pleistocene) in Argentina. Our analysis demonstrates that the type material of N. rudis belongs to a juvenile specimen of Panochthus Burmeister 1866. A comparative examination of caudal tubes in Panochthus reveals the ontogenetic sequence of this structure, representing the most complete developmental record described for glyptodonts to date. Most of the taxa traditionally assigned to the tribe Neuryurini (Neuryurus, Urotherium Castellanos 1926 and Pseudoeuryurus Ameghino 1889) are reinterpreted as juvenile or taphonomically altered specimens. This revision clarifies that the diversity of Late Pleistocene glyptodonts in southern South America (i.e. Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and southern Brazil and Bolivia) is restricted to four species: Neosclerocalyptus paskoensis (Zurita 2002), Doedicurus clavicaudatus (Owen 1847), Glyptodon reticulatus Owen 1845, and Panochthus tuberculatus Burmeister 1866.
items.summary: 《对令人困惑的雕齿兽类的重新审视：Neuryurus rudis（Gervais）及其对Panochthus个体发育的启示》：研究重新修订了阿根廷Ensenadan期的Neuryurus rudis，证明其模式材料属于Panochthus的幼年个体，并揭示Panochthus尾管的个体发育序列，将Neuryurini族多数类群重新解释为幼年或埋藏改造标本，…
items.title: A review of confusing glyptodonts: Neuryurus rudis (Gervais) (Xenarthra: Glyptodontidae) and its implications for the ontogeny of Panochthus Burmeister

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The ‘Palaeogene strata’ of the Itaboraí Basin (upper Paleocene‐lower Eocene), Southeastern Brazil, has preserved 29 genera and almost 50 species of metatherians (about 65% of its mammalian diversity). Among them,
                    <jats:italic>Eobrasilia coutoi</jats:italic>
                    Simpson, 1947 is the most enigmatic due to its quite fragmentary nature. We redescribe this species by assigning new molars, first micro‐CT and microwear data, and reinterpreting its systematic affinities.
                    <jats:italic>Eobrasilia coutoi</jats:italic>
                    weighed about 5.92 kg, thus representing the largest Palaeogene non‐sparassodont metatherian from South America and Antarctica. A phylogenetic analysis recovered
                    <jats:italic>Eobrasilia</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Periprotodidelphis</jats:italic>
                    as sister taxa (Eobrasiliidae rank nov.) within Polydolopimorphia. Lower molars morphofunctional variables (talonid relative area and height, and width by the length of the lower molar) suggest that
                    <jats:italic>E. coutoi</jats:italic>
                    has a pattern more similar to that of extant New World Primates (Cebidae, Pitheciidae) than extant didelphids. Buccolingually oriented wear facets on the parastyle and postmetacrista suggest a developed ectental masticatory component. Its microwear pattern is characterized by a predominance of fine scratches and small pits, resembling the pattern of callitrichids and cebids but differing from these in having longer scratches.
                    <jats:italic>Eobrasilia coutoi</jats:italic>
                    was likely a sclerocarpophagous metatherian, being able to exploit unripe fruits and seeds as food; however, it cannot be considered a specialized durophagous/hard‐object feeder like extant pitheciines. The results suggest a Tropical humid ‘mammalian trophic biome’ for the localities in the Itaboraí Basin with
                    <jats:italic>Eobrasilia coutoi</jats:italic>
                    . This is consistent with an early Eocene age (likely contemporaneous to the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum) inferred for Itaboraí youngest faunal assemblage.
                  </jats:p>
items.summary: 《南美洲古近纪独特硬果食性后兽类Eobrasilia coutoi（后兽亚纲：多门齿兽形类）的再描述：系统亲缘关系及古生态与演化意义》：该研究通过新增臼齿标本、首次显微CT与微磨痕数据，重新描述了巴西Itaboraí盆地古新世晚期至始新世早期这一最神秘的后兽类，估算其体重约5.92公斤，并分析其系统位置与食性，值得古生物与演化生物学读者关注。
items.title: Redescription of † Eobrasilia coutoi ( Metatheria : Polydolopimorphia ), a unique sclerocarpophagous metatherian from the Palaeogene of South America : Systematic affinities, and paleoecological and evolutionary implications

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Cranial bones of squamate reptiles diverge in shape and structure across lineages, while preserving the basic skull plan. Therefore, variation in cranial morphology of squamates is key to understanding phylogenetic relationships, species delimitation, and lifestyles, which ultimately contribute to insights into their evolution and ecology. Nevertheless, although Gymnophthalmidae is the most diverse endemic non‐ophidian squamate family in the Neotropics, studies on comparative cranial osteology within this lineage remain scarce. Herein, we thoroughly describe and compare the external skull anatomy of six species of the Andean genus
                    <jats:italic>Riama</jats:italic>
                    from Colombia and Ecuador (
                    <jats:italic>R. columbiana</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>R. simotera</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>R. striata</jats:italic>
                    , and three undescribed taxa), aiming to provide phenotypic evidence for phylogenetic, taxonomic, and functional analyses. We examined 12 cleared‐and‐stained skulls of adult specimens (one male and one female per species) to preliminarily assess inter‐ and intraspecific variation within
                    <jats:italic>Riama</jats:italic>
                    . Interspecific variation occurs in the degree of contact between nasals (and consequently in the articulation of the nasal process of the premaxilla), and in the absence/presence of the posterior process of the jugal, among others. An anterior process of the ventral crest of the vomer in female
                    <jats:italic>R. columbiana</jats:italic>
                    is seemingly unique among gymnophthalmids. The number of tooth positions and teeth morphology vary both among sexes and species. Preliminary evidence implies sexual dimorphism and bilateral variation in some characters. Our findings suggest that variation in skull anatomy within
                    <jats:italic>Riama</jats:italic>
                    can inform species delimitation, and phylogenetic and functional analyses. Finally, we discuss variation in cranial morphology among species of
                    <jats:italic>Riama</jats:italic>
                    within a phylogenetic context.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Yuly A. Vega‐Rangel, Sandy Escobar‐Maestre, Teddy Angarita‐Sierra, Santiago J. Sánchez‐Pacheco

items.title: Cranial osteology of Neotropical squamate reptiles of the genus Riama (Gymnophthalmidae: Cercosaurinae)
